newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Strikes mark 24th day of Bulgarian mass protests.
newsitem.headline: Strikes mark 24th day of Bulgarian mass protests.

text.p: Bulgarians held anti-government strikes and rallies on Wednesday or queued to change fast-depreciating savings to dollars as political and economic crisis deepened on the 24th day of mass protests.
One-hour strikes disrupted schools, factories and railways around the country, but public transport ran normally in Sofia and airports were open.
Four cars and a few protesters caused traffic chaos in central Sofia by blocking the street outside the headquarters of the main opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF).
The three main trade unions called for strikes after the ex-communist Socialists insisted they would form a new cabinet despite popular pressure for an immediate election.
Outside the capital, one-hour blockades closed several main roads. Church bells tolled in the town of Doupnitsa, where a shoe factory stopped work for an hour.
The main branch of the State Savings Bank in Sofia was crammed with depositors trying to withdraw savings losing their value by the hour.
The lev fell to new lows of 1,300-1,500 per dollar on the interbank market but dealers said almost no one was trading in the present uncertainty.
"I am fed up with all this chaos and I do not trust politicians, so it would be better to withdraw my levs and buy some dollars," said Michail Shopov.
"I do not care that the dollar is at 1,500 now. Last week, when I could buy dollars at 800-900, I decided to wait for some time and I was wrong."

Wages have been increased in a few key sectors to ward off strikes and compensate for inflation, forecast at 50 percent for January alone, but many Bulgarians are struggling to make ends meet. Shopkeepers in some poorer districts say they are selling little more than bread and yoghurt.

"We were told that our wages were doubled but the increase won't come through for a month and by then who knows what the lev-dollar rate will be," said ticket seller Lilia Nikolova at Sofia's main station, where trains sounded their horns at 10 a.m. (0900 GMT) to mark the start of their strike.

"We are suffering enough, now we have to suffer more because of this chaos. I heard that their pay demands have been met, what else do they want?" said traveller Angel Dilianov, who missed his connection in Plovdiv because of the strike.
After failing to find a compromise between the warring political factions, President Petar Stoyanov on Tuesday asked Socialist interior minister Nikolai Dobrev to form a new government.

The UDF said it would suspend its boycott of parliament to try to stop Dobrev from winning approval for a cabinet. Although the Socialists have an absolute majority, the UDF hopes for defections from party ranks.

Under the constitution, Stoyanov had to give the mandate to the Socialists -- parliament's biggest party and the caretaker government since Socialist prime minister Zhan Videnov resigned on December 21.
The opposition wants an immediate general election, while the Socialists are proposing polls in the autumn, more than a year before their mandate expires in December 1998.
Sofia students plan a torchlight rally on Wednesday evening and a contest to choose Miss Protest and Mr Vagabond -- critics of their inventive daily rallies have called them "mere vagabonds".
